status: cross-simulator measurement discrepancy; operational transfer open
claim: iFogSim reports edge-ward placement reducing modeled latency, network use, and cloud energy while slightly increasing edge energy in two simulated applications. A later independent YAFS comparison of the same EEG-game placement scenario reports broadly similar trends but non-identical outputs and identifies differences in resource units, link/propagation delay, and event semantics; its dynamic scenarios use arbitrary parameter values without real-trace validation. Thus placement conclusions need matched simulator and real-system calibration, and cloud-only energy is not a sufficient system-wide outcome.

sources.title: iFogSim: A Toolkit for Modeling and Simulation of Resource Management Techniques in Internet of Things, Edge and Fog Computing Environments
locators: §§5–6: EEG and surveillance simulated case studies; edge-ward placement results for latency, network use, cloud and edge energy
§6.3: simulator RAM/runtime measured on the selected simulation configurations

sources.title: YAFS: A simulator for IoT scenarios in fog computing
locators: §4, Tables 2–3: same EEG-game placement policies; cross-simulator numerical differences and latency convergence over 50 runs
§4: MIPS/IPT, bandwidth, propagation delay, and event-semantics mismatch explanations
§5: dynamic scenarios use arbitrary parameters and lack real-case comparison

interpretation: This is a concrete warning that matched placement trends can coexist with simulator-dependent numeric estimates. It does not establish that edge placement usually loses energy or that one simulator is categorically wrong.
falsifiable_question: Under identical public IoT traces, device/link parameters, task-success criteria, and calibrated power models, do two independent simulators and a small real testbed agree on the direction and magnitude of cloud-only versus edge-ward effects for latency, dropped tasks, bytes transferred, and total joules per successful task? Which modeling conventions change policy rankings?
primary_outcome: Paired effect of placement policy on end-to-end joules per successful task, with latency, network bytes, task failures, and simulator runtime/memory as separate outcomes.
counterevidence_and_caveats: The iFogSim and YAFS comparison is one application model, not a broad multi-workload replication.
Different computational units and network semantics may explain some differences; neither paper establishes ground truth for production deployments.
YAFS authors say the dynamic-feature scenarios could not be compared with real cases and use arbitrary parameter distributions.
suggested_design: Select an openly traceable IoT workload; publish a single canonical parameter manifest and mapping to each simulator; calibrate device and network behavior on a small testbed; run paired cloud/edge policies with repeated seeds; report total and per-tier energy, latency, drops, bytes, and simulator resource cost.

status: cross-benchmark measurement warning; matched causal test open
claim: Two MCP-agent benchmarks distinguish syntactically or operationally valid tool calls from end-to-end task correctness. MCP-Radar reports a file-management condition with 84.5% GPT-4o valid tool-call rate but 43% answer accuracy; InfoMosaic-Bench reports domain-dependent effects of adding tools and attributes 22.4% of failures to tool selection/use. These results suggest tool routing and evidence integration can bottleneck success after invocation, but the benchmarks are not directly comparable.

sources.title: MCP-Radar: A Multi-Domain Benchmark for Assessing Tool-Use Capabilities of Large Language Models
locators: §5 / Table 3: valid-call and final-accuracy gap, including file-management result

sources.title: InfoMosaic-Bench: Evaluating Tool-Augmented LLMs Across Domains
locators: §§5.2–5.3: domain variation from tool augmentation and 22.4% tool-selection/use error category

interpretation: The cross-paper synthesis supports a measurement caution and a falsifiable bottleneck hypothesis, not a causal claim that more tools hurt or a direct comparison of reported percentages.
falsifiable_question: On matched tasks with a fixed model, tool set, and call/token budget, does explicit stagewise tool routing, schema feedback, and evidence integration improve end-to-end task correctness beyond merely increasing valid calls, especially for multi-source tasks?
primary_outcome: End-to-end exact/task success; secondary outcomes separately score tool selection, schema-valid invocation, retrieved-evidence relevance, and evidence-supported final answer.
counterevidence_and_caveats: The benchmark tasks, models, domains, and metrics differ, so headline rates are not direct effect comparisons.
Tool availability effects vary by domain; do not assume a universal benefit or harm from adding tools.
The suggested planning intervention has not been tested by these results; its effectiveness remains unknown.
suggested_design: Build paired tasks with identical evidence/tool affordances; compare baseline routing with stagewise route-call-verify-integrate, equalize tool and token budgets, randomize task seeds, and report each pipeline stage plus end-to-end success by domain and number of required sources.
